title: Kintsugi: Gate Low-Bit Quantization on Tasks, Not on Average Error Alone
description: Low-bit quantization of language models is usually tuned on an average error, such as the KL divergence to the full-precision model. The Kintsugi method gates every change on task probes next to KL, with each pass line written before its run, and confirms on data that no choice used. On two models that fit one 12 GB GPU: (1) On Qwen3.8-27B at temperature 1.0, a 2.47-bit build scores above BF16 on AppWorld test_challenge on four of four seeds (+117 of 1,668 task-runs; seed-level p = 5.1e-4), also in BF16's setup. Almost all of the gap is one end-of-task habit of the base model: on an action task, the run passes an unasked answer and fails. BF16 does this in 258 runs, the build in 112; with these runs counted as passes (a post hoc class), the two are level. At temperature 0 the lead is +11 [-5, +28]. Reasoning effort xhigh lowers the habit (3 against 13 runs on a targeted set); one targeted sentence does not. (2) Average KL does not rank bit maps: six maps of one size score 586 to 680 of 834. A class-level KL table found a repair worth 70 task-runs, and 8 raised projections carry it. (3) Lines written before the runs held two lower-KL maps out of the release. (4) On Inkling 2 Mini, another lineage, our build scores above a public 2-bit file with the setup equal (598 against 579 of 672; p = 0.019); the 27B allocation rule did not carry over. We did not invent the quantizer, the trellis codec or the 27B bit allocation.
